newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch share market fall seen as healthy correction.
newsitem.headline: Dutch share market fall seen as healthy correction.

text.p: A 10 percent plunge from all-time highs on the Amsterdam bourse over the last 10 days has been a healthy correction in a market that had been losing touch with fundamentals, analysts said on Friday.
The market bounced back 2.8 percent by mid afternoon on Friday, recouping much of Thursday's spectacular tumble when the market suffered one of its largest ever one-day losses.
But dealers said the market remained nervous with an options expiry on Friday dragging the physical market around, although there was a feeling that Thursday's dive had been overdone.

On Thursday the AEX index of 25 leading shares hit a day's low of 700.54 points on speculation that U.S. interest rates were set to rise, before rebounding a little to close 3.36 percent lower at 710.31.
This compares with the record of 779.02 on March 11, the culmination of a climb from 648 at the end of 1996 which was fuelled by a strong Dutch economy and company earnings.

"We view this as a healthy correction to a market that was overheating. The AEX has let off some steam and looks fairly based to consolidate around 720 for the time being," said Kees de Vaan of MeesPierson.
By mid-afternoon on Friday the index was around 730.

"The mood is still very nervous, particularly ahead of the options expiry. But generally the feeling is yesterday's move was overdone and the panic selling we saw was all on the back of options and futures," one trader said.

ING Barings said that despite the correction, Amsterdam shares are not cheap. The market, like those throughout much of the developed world, remains worried whether the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will raise interest rates when it meets on March 25.

"Despite a 10 percent drop since its all-time high last Tuesday, the Dutch equity market is still not a bargain...If the FOMC decides to raise official rates by 50 basis points next week, the bottom will move a little more south," ING Barings said in a research note.

"On the other hand, as most selling pressure stems from private investors and domestic institutional investors are cautiously operating on the buy side, the downward risk might be modest," ING Barings added.

Analysts said part of Thursday's panic on the Amsterdam bourse, where trading was briefly suspended in options and some forms of equity deals, was because options operators were scrambling to unwind positions before expiry.
"Everthing seems a bit exaggerated so far. I guess we have seen the bottom for the moment at 700 on the AEX," said De Vaan.
Dennis Ederzeel, equities strategist at Delta Lloyd Bank, also welcomed the drop. "When we reached the level of 770 we lost every connection with the interest rates, with the real economy," said.
"The market is quite expensive but it's more back to normal levels. As the interest rates are rising now you can expect it maybe to go a little bit lower," he added.
Part of Thursday's spasm was due to Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan stressing the importance of prompt action to keep inflation down before it hurts the economy.
De Vaan estimated Greenspan's remarks accounted for about 15 points of Thursday's fall.

"If you look at the other exchanges around Europe they were off around 1.5 percent. We were down more because we have risen more (recently). Valuations here are more extreme than all the others," he said.
Analysts have criticised the recent Dutch market euphoria which has been boosted by private investors and a flood of plentiful institutional liquidity.
Some of Thursday's fall was also due to bearish press comment saying that foreign securities houses were saying the Dutch market was vulnerable to a big setback.

"We were underweight on our European portfolio anyway," said Richard Davidson, European equities strategist at Morgan Stanley in London. "But on Monday I put out a very bearish piece on the Netherlands saying in effect that the (Dutch) interest rate rises we've seen since the beginning of this year are only the beginning of a much bigger trend."
"Although we don't expect the guilder to get significantly weaker, we think the strength of the economy is presaging inflationary pressures further down the line," he added.
Bryan Allworthy, European equities strategist at Merrill Lynch in London, said the AEX looked fully valued at 720.
"From the peaks of 10 days ago it would be healthy to get a 10-15 percent correction in equity markets just to get some order and some structure back into the market," he said.

"It's been a liquidity rally so far this year and that is very much dependent on sentiment, they (investors) are just taking stock and taking profits and are going to re-evaluate the situation," said Allworthy.
